Subject: Discovery: Cadenza Health — logging guardrails & PII handling (recap + next steps)

Hi Laura / Tom — thanks again for the call today. Quick written recap so we have alignment and clear next steps. Notes below are based on our conversation and Sean/Monica's live clarifications. Please correct anything I misunderstood.

Summary of main pain points
- You need strict control over logging to avoid storing PII from patient notes and PHI-derived identifiers in long-term logs.
- Current vendor logs are retained indefinitely; your security policy requires short retention windows and redact-at-ingest for anything that looks like a national ID or SSN equivalent.
- Auditability: auditors ask for tamper-evident, exportable audit logs showing model version, input fingerprint (hash), and user ID mapping (pseudonymized).

Success criteria (what would make a pilot successful)
1) End-to-end demo showing redaction-at-ingest and zero retention of raw PII after 30 days.
2) Audit log export that contains model/version, timestamp, operation id, and a SHA256 hash of the original input (not the raw text).
3) Configuration in the console to enforce redaction rules and retention policy per customer (not global).

Current stack you described
- App tier: Node.js microservices on AWS ECS
- Logging: Splunk Enterprise (ingest agent currently captures request bodies)
- Identity: Okta SSO; user IDs are stable but you require pseudonymization in logs

Immediate constraints flagged on the call
- No raw PHI in persistent logs beyond 30 days.
- Where possible, redaction must occur prior to any long-term storage or third-party forwarding.
- For compliance, you must be able to provide per-request proof the redaction took place (audit chain).

Attachments I’m sending (short stubs)
- redwood-soc2-questionnaire.pdf (SOC 2 / security questionnaire answers)
- cadenza-logging-requirements.xlsx (summary spreadsheet of retention & redaction rules we captured)

Proposed next steps
- Sean to share a short technical note showing how redaction-at-ingest would sit in your call path (expected by Tue 27 Apr).
- Cadenza to confirm which identifiers count as PII for you (e.g., MRN, SSN, insurance policy numbers) — Laura/Tom to send list by Tue 27 Apr.
- Align on pilot scope: low-volume production sandbox (30k tokens/day) for 2 weeks. Rachel to draft SOW outline and budget.

If that looks right I’ll schedule a follow-up technical session with Sean and your security contact on Wed/Thu next week.

Thanks —

Laura — adding a few technical notes ahead of the follow-up: attaching a short technical sketch and checklist as promised. High-level answers to your questions below.

How redaction-at-ingest would look (two patterns)
1) Inline redaction (preferred when latency budget allows): request body passes through a redaction filter before any log sink. Filter emits redacted payload to the app and writes a redaction event to the audit log (includes rule id and original-hash).
2) Sidecar redaction: if you cannot change the request path, a sidecar captures the incoming request, performs deterministic redaction and writes redacted payloads to Splunk while raw input is dropped after a transient buffer.

Audit log contents (minimum)
- timestamp, request_id, model, model_version, operation, user_pseudonym, redaction_rule_id, input_sha256, redaction_delta (summary), retention_policy_id

Data retention controls
- Per-tenant retention policies supported; defaults can be set per environment. We can automatically delete raw inputs after N days and keep only redaction events/hashes for M days.

I'll put the technical sketch in the shared Drive folder and drop the SOC2 answers PDF. Proposed time for follow-up tech session: Thu 29 Apr 10:00–11:00 PT. Confirmable if that works for your security team.
